Subject: weird question
Hi Nitin bhai,
Something strange happened today. Ammi asked me to fetch the pickle jar from the back storeroom, and I just stood outside the door. My hands went cold. I went back and said I couldn't find it.
That's the room where Abbu and Chacha had the big fight at Eid last year. Everyone keeps saying how awful it was, but honestly I remember almost nothing. Maybe a plate breaking? That's it.
Same with the old song that was playing that day. When it came on in the car on Sunday, I didn't say a word for the whole drive and didn't know why.
You were there. Was it really that bad? You're the only one I feel I can ask.
Hafsa

qa.q: What was Hafsa asked to fetch from the storeroom?
qa.a: The pickle jar.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa's hands go cold outside the storeroom?
qa.a: The room seems tied to the fight Hafsa can barely remember; the hurt is still there, so the body tenses even though the memory has gone.

qa.q: What choice in the email could help Hafsa start to understand the feeling, and what else might help?
qa.a: Asking Nitin, someone trusted who was there, is a good first step; talking it through with Ammi or a school counsellor could help too.

qa.q: How might Nitin feel reading 'You're the only one I feel I can ask'?
qa.a: Nitin may feel trusted but also careful, wanting to answer gently about a fight that was hard for the whole family.

grounding: A teenager emails a cousin about barely remembering a bitter family fight while going tense at the storeroom and the song from that day.

"Sonali, why did you just vanish from my party?"
Okay, Saurabh. Here's the honest answer, and it's weird. When you put on that old film song, the one with the violins, I just went cold. I sat on your balcony and couldn't talk.
Mum says that song was on the TV the night she and Papa had the huge fight, before Papa moved to Pune for a while. Everyone in the family still talks about that night. I was thirteen. I remember the TV. I remember my cousin's sandals by the door. That's it. The shouting? Nothing. It's just gone.
But my stomach knows the song, apparently. I'm not making this up, I promise.
So, sorry about your party. Could we maybe skip that one next time?

qa.q: What song was playing when Sonali went cold?
qa.a: That old film song, the one with the violins.

qa.q: Why does Sonali say 'my stomach knows the song'?
qa.a: Sonali feels anxious and tense when the song plays; the fight itself is gone from memory, but the body reacts before the mind can explain it.

qa.q: What step did Sonali take that could help, and what else might?
qa.a: Explaining honestly to Saurabh and asking to skip the song was practical; talking to Mum or a school counsellor about that night could help with the stored hurt.

qa.q: How might Saurabh feel hearing why Sonali left the party?
qa.a: Saurabh may feel relieved it had nothing to do with the party, and glad to be trusted with something so personal.

My brother Uday is sixteen. Since the fight in the living room last Diwali, when Dadi and Papa shouted about selling the village house, he does his homework on our bedroom floor, never on the sofa. When I asked him about that night, he said, "Honestly, I don't remember much. Was it loud?" I believe him. He looked genuinely confused.
But on Sunday Papa played the old devotional song that was on that night, and Uday went quiet, shoulders up by his ears, and walked out in the middle of a sentence.
I don't know what's happening inside him. I've started closing the living-room door when that song plays.
— Pallavi

qa.a: The hurt from that night seems stored away without the memory, so the living room still feels uneasy to Uday though he can't say why.

qa.q: How is the fight still affecting Pallavi?

Sunday: At Mehr's cousin's wedding in Amritsar, the DJ played an old Punjabi song. Mehr, sixteen, set down her plate and went to the car. Her brother Tushar found her there, staring at the dashboard. "You okay?" "Headache."
Wednesday: At home, Tushar asked, "You remember the night of the big fight? Dad and Chachaji, in the drawing room, when the plates broke?" Mehr frowned. "Not really. Some shouting? I don't remember much." She honestly didn't.
Two weeks later: Mehr had to fetch a book from the drawing room. She stopped at the door. Her hand tightened on the frame and she went very quiet. The same song was playing from Tushar's phone. "Switch it off," she said sharply. Tushar did. He was about to explain, then just said, "Okay." Mehr went in, grabbed the book, and left fast.

qa.q: Where did the big family fight happen?
qa.a: In the drawing room, when the plates broke.

qa.q: Why did Mehr go quiet at the drawing room door?
qa.a: The room and the song seemed to bring back the hurt from the fight, even though she couldn't clearly remember the night itself.

qa.q: What choice did Tushar make at the door, and why was it sensible?
qa.a: He switched off the song and just said "Okay" instead of explaining, letting Mehr feel safe without forcing the memory on her.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel noticing a pattern his sister cannot see?
qa.a: Tushar seems to understand what the song and room mean, and may feel worried and protective, unsure how or when to talk about it.

passage: Darshan, I saw you leave the room when that song came on at Nani's. Sit with your Urmila Mausi a minute; you're my only nephew, after all. When I was fifteen, there was a terrible fight in our house in Nashik. Your Nana and his brother, over the shop. Doors banging, words I won't repeat. The next year, if anyone asked, I truly couldn't tell you much. A bit of shouting, maybe. But whenever I walked into our front room, I'd go stiff and quiet. And whenever the radio played the song that was on that night, I'd find a reason to leave. I thought I'd just moved on. Years later, talking with a friend, it all came back in one piece: the room, the song, how scared I'd been. It wasn't gone, beta. Only put on a shelf. You can talk to me about anything on your shelf.

passage: The Kolkata flat was quiet on Sunday, and Vishal put on the radio while he washed the dishes. The old Rabindrasangeet came on, the one their mother used to hum. Trisha, sitting at the dining table with her homework, stopped writing. Her jaw set. "Turn it off," she said. "Why? It's nice." "Just turn it off." Vishal turned it off and looked at her. She was gripping her pen. "What's wrong?" "Nothing." And she meant it; she couldn't have said. Last winter there had been a terrible fight at this table, Ma and Baba and Dida, voices she'd never heard before, and the song had been on then too. Trisha remembered almost nothing of what was said. She just knew she didn't like sitting here with that song. She picked up her books and moved to her room.

qa.a: He could gently mention it later, when things are calm, and ask if something about that song bothers her, or suggest she talk to a trusted adult.

"Preeti, come in! Mum's making chai."
"Thanks, Parveen."
The radio in Parveen's kitchen was playing an old film song. Preeti stopped in the doorway.
"Can you... change that?"
"The song? Why?"
"I don't know. I just don't like it."
Parveen switched stations. "You went all stiff."
"Did I?" Preeti rubbed her arms. "It's weird. Papa used to play it. And there was that fight, the night Dadi left our house. I don't even remember what anyone said. I just remember the song."
"You never told me about that."
"There's nothing to tell. I don't remember it." Preeti laughed, but it came out wrong.
Parveen handed her a cup. "Okay. But if you ever do want to tell, I'm here."
"Mm." Preeti held the cup with both hands.

qa.a: She switched stations.

qa.a: Preeti felt uneasy and hurt underneath; the fight was shelved in her memory but the pain was still there, so trying to laugh it off didn't work.

There was a big fight at home last year, in the living room, the night Papa and Ma argued about moving to Delhi. Everyone shouted. My brother Wasim told me later that I cried and slammed the door.

The strange thing is, I honestly don't remember most of it. Just a blur.

But whenever I sit on that sofa, my shoulders go tight and I want to leave. And when the old film song that was playing on the TV that night comes on the radio, I switch it off before I know why.

Last week Wasim asked if I was okay. I said yes. But maybe the hurt is still there, just shelved.

I'm Seema. I think I might talk to Ma about it this weekend.

School counsellor's note, Tuesday.

Rehana, class ten, was referred by her teacher because she walked out of the music room today when a particular song played. She said she didn't know why she left. She said she just felt "really weird and tight."

With her permission, I asked about home. She mentioned there'd been a very bad argument between her parents some months ago but said, "I don't really remember it. It was loud." Her friend Indu, who waited outside, told me that song had been playing at the family's party that night.

Rehana seems to have shelved the hurt without dealing with it. I've offered her weekly sessions, and with her agreement I called her mother this afternoon to talk about support at home.

qa.a: She walked out of the music room today when a particular song played.

qa.q: How did Rehana describe her feeling when she walked out?

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor take?
qa.a: Offered weekly sessions and, with Rehana's agreement, called her mother that afternoon to talk about support at home.

qa.a: Indu probably felt worried and caring, which is why Indu shared what was known about the song.

Saturday

Went to Preeti's house today. Her mum put on an old song while cooking and I suddenly felt awful. My chest went tight and I wanted to cry.

Preeti asked, "What's wrong?" I said, "Nothing." But I had to go to the bathroom and breathe.

At home Mum told me that song was playing on the night of the big fight between her and Nani last Diwali. Everyone shouted. I stood in the kitchen doorway.

I don't really remember it. Just shouting. But my body does, I guess.

Mum hugged me and said we'd talk more tomorrow, and that I can always tell her when something like this happens.

— Hansa

When her friend Yosef came over for a school project, he spread their papers on the dining-room table. Lindiwe stood in the doorway and didn't come in. Her shoulders were up near her ears. "Can we work in the kitchen?" she asked. "Sure, but why?" She honestly didn't know. Her aunt, passing by, touched her arm. "Still that room, my girl?" Her aunt said, "Your mind put it away. It still needs talking about, when you're ready."
